title: Posing
subtitle: The half of the dance an audience actually remembers.
description: Tyrone Proctor put the order as "posing came first, followed by waacking, then voguing" — the held shapes are older than the arm work bolted onto them. A pose is not a freeze: it tells a story and carries a personality, and the originators borrowed theirs from the screen icons they grew up watching. This is the cheapest thing on the whole path to get good at, and the most neglected.

stages.title: Shapes
stages.description: Start with poses somebody else already made work, then build your own.

steps.title: Screen-icon poses
steps.description: Four shapes drawn from old Hollywood glamour — the dress, the over-the-shoulder, the chin-up. Strike from neutral and hold for a full eight counts; the holding is the hard part.

steps.title: Four poses, four words
steps.description: Build four poses of your own and give each one a word or a sound. Saying the intention out loud changes what the body does — it is the difference between a shape and a character.

steps.title: Hair brushes and face frames
steps.description: The small gestures that carry character between the big shapes. Almost never drilled, and the first thing that makes a freestyle look inhabited rather than assembled.

stages.title: Using them
stages.description: A pose in a drill is a shape. A pose on a break is a moment.

steps.title: Pose on three levels
steps.description: The same four poses standing, crouched and on the floor. Height is the cheapest variety in the dance and the easiest to forget you have.

steps.title: Land it on the break
steps.description: Hold the shape exactly where the record stops. Landing early reads as a guess and landing late reads as a stumble — this is a listening exercise more than a movement one.

steps.title: Hold it through the phrase
steps.description: Stay in the pose for a full eight after you hit it, face and all, without checking whether it worked. Most dancers break the shape a beat early; the audience is still looking.
